newsitem.title: USA: Dollar closes firmer in U.S., holds near 113 yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes firmer in U.S., holds near 113 yen.

text.p: *Dollar ends U.S. session near 113 yen, well-supported near 22-month high. Dlr/mark battered, but holds ground near 1.52. *Mark enjoys late boost after BoI 75-bp rate cut. Mark/lira rises toward 1007, hurts dollar/mark. Big mark/lira cap 1010. *Buba Issing statement no German rate cut ahead propels mark. *Wire report unnamed U.S. aide doubts dollar to deepen trade gap.
Dollar/mark closed higher, but near overnight lows Wednesday after Bundesbank officials said they saw no need to cut interest rates, dealers said.
Dollar/yen also rose, aided by an unconfirmed report U.S. officials do not fear a firm dollar will widen the trade gap.
Otmar Issing, chief economist at Germany's central bank, said in a German television interview that he saw no reason to expect lower interest rates.
Later, Bundesbank vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said current German interest rates were appropriate and that the Bundesbank wants to keep them steady as long as possible.
The mark surged after the Issing report, reaching its highest level in three and a half years at 74.26 yen, and also gaining on the dollar.
"We continue to see tremendous demand for marks, especially against the yen. It's coming from every sector of the world," said John Hazelton, chief currency dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.

The dollar rose to 1.5210/20 marks from 1.5200/10 at the open. The dollar rebounded from early lows against the yen to break 113 yen for the first time in 33 months, ending at 112.90/00 yen, up from 112.65/75 at the open.
The dollar also slumped against the yen in early trading, but later rebounded on comments from Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita.
Matsushita told a meeting of Bank of Japan deputies that the Japanese economy would likely grow slowly and that market expectations for higher Japanese interest rates had abated.
"It's not so much dollar strength as it is yen weakness that we're seeing," said John Gariano, vice president at Sumitomo Bank New York.
A report from financial news agency Bridge News, appeared to accelerate dollar buying in U.S. trading, dealers said.
Bridge quoted an unidentified source claiming the Clinton Administration did not fear the firming dollar will expand the bilateral trade deficit with Japan, which has fallen lately.
As the dollar rises against the yen, U.S. exports to Japan become more expensive, while Japanese import prices fall.
Administration officials have consistently stated in public that they want a strong dollar.
But another anonymous news report Tuesday claimed the Administration feared the rising dollar would worsen the trade picture. Wednesday's report seemed to refute that story.
"It was a contradiction of the statement (Tuesday), and it gave the dollar room to go back up again," said Vincent Amaru, a foreign exchange vice president at Citibank.
Late in New York trading, the mark got a modest boost from the Bank of Italy, which announced a surprising cut in its key discount rate to 7.5 percent from 8.25 percent.
The mark climbed against the lira and also rose against the dollar.
"The mark remains strong against everything. The dollar is just holding its own," said Amaru.
The dollar ended higher at 1.2535/45 Swiss francs from 1.2495/05 at the open. Sterling fell to $1.5965/70 from $1.5990/00.
The dollar slipped to Canadian $1.3436/41 from C$1.3461/66. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7938/43 from $0.7945/50.
--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664
